segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The beginning of the good news of Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Just as it is written in Isaiah the prophet:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Look, I am sending my messenger ahead of you, who will prepare your way;

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: a voice of one crying out in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight,’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so John the Baptizer appeared in the wilderness, proclaiming a baptism of turning back for the forgiveness of sins.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the whole Judean countryside and all the people of Jerusalem were going out to him, and they were being baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: John was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he proclaimed,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “One who is stronger than I is coming after me; I am not fit to stoop down and untie the strap of his sandals.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In those days it happened that Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized in the Jordan by John.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And at once, as he was coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit, like a dove, coming down on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And a voice came from the heavens:

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “You are my Son, the beloved; in you I delight.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And at once the Spirit drove him out into the wilderness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was in the wilderness forty days, being tested by Satan; he was with the wild animals, and the angels were serving him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After John had been handed over, Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the good news of God

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The time has been fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near. Turn back, and believe in the good news.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was passing along beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew, Simon’s brother, casting a net in the sea, for they were fishers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And at once they left their nets and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and his brother John, who were in their boat mending the nets,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and at once he called them. And they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men and went off after him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They went into Capernaum, and at once, on the Sabbath, he began teaching in the synagogue.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were astounded at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes did.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Just then there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit, and he cried out,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What do you want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus rebuked him, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Be silent, and come out of him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the unclean spirit threw him into convulsions, cried out with a loud voice, and came out of him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were all so amazed that they began asking one another,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “What is this? A new teaching! With authority he commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And at once the report about him went out everywhere, through the whole surrounding region of Galilee.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And at once, on leaving the synagogue, they went to the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Simon’s mother-in-law was lying down with a fever, and at once they told him about her.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He came to her, took her by the hand, and raised her up; the fever left her, and she began serving them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When evening came, after the sun had set, people were bringing to him all who were sick and those possessed by demons,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the whole town was gathered at the door.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He healed many who were sick with various diseases and drove out many demons, and he would not let the demons speak, because they knew him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he got up, went out, and went away to a deserted place, and there he was praying.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon and those with him tracked him down,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and when they found him they said to him,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “Everyone is looking for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Let us go elsewhere, into the neighboring towns, so that I may proclaim there too, for that is what I came out to do.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he went through the whole of Galilee, proclaiming in their synagogues and driving out the demons.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A man with leprosy came to him, begging him and kneeling down, and saying to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you are willing, you can make me clean.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Angered, he stretched out his hand, touched him, and said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am willing; be made clean.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And at once the leprosy left him, and he was made clean.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And warning him sternly, he sent him away at once,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he went out and began to proclaim it at length and to spread the story, so that Jesus could no longer enter a town openly, but stayed outside in deserted places; and people kept coming to him from everywhere.

notes.note: The traditional rendering is 'gospel', which today suggests a religious term or the title of a book. In the first century the word was an ordinary one for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between 'gospel' and 'good news'.

notes.traditional: Jesus Christ, the Son of God
notes.note: Most manuscripts continue with 'Son of God', and most English translations include it. The words are missing from a few early witnesses, including the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, and the SBLGNT text translated here omits them. Scholars are divided on whether the phrase was dropped by accident or added by a copyist.

Only the lines in verse 3 come from Isaiah (40:3). The lines in verse 2 blend Exodus 23:20 and Malachi 3:1. Many later manuscripts read 'in the prophets', probably to smooth this over, which is why older English versions have that wording.

The traditional rendering is 'repentance' (and 'repent' in verse 15), which in modern English centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term understood to include a change of life.

notes.phrase: a leather belt around his waist
notes.note: The description echoes that of the prophet Elijah in 2 Kings 1:8, a hairy garment and a leather belt. A reader who knew the Scriptures would have caught the hint that John comes in the role of Elijah, whose return was expected before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5).

The Greek is plural here and in verse 11, a Semitic turn of phrase that many translations flatten to 'heaven', at least in verse 11. The plural is kept in both places. The verb 'torn open' is a violent one, and may echo the plea of Isaiah 64:1 that God would tear the heavens and come down.

Mark's preposition usually means 'into' or 'to', whereas Matthew and Luke use the word for 'upon'. Some scholars take Mark to mean that the Spirit entered Jesus. In everyday Greek of the period the preposition was often used loosely for motion toward or onto something, and the image of a dove suits alighting, so the traditional sense is kept here.

The traditional rendering is 'tempted'. The Greek verb means to put to the test, whether with good or hostile intent, and the forty days in the wilderness recall Israel's testing there. 'Tempted' narrows this to enticement to sin, which is part of the meaning but not the whole of it.

Most translations say John was 'arrested' or 'put in prison', which is what happened. The Greek verb is simply 'handed over', and it is the same verb Mark later uses again and again for Jesus being handed over to his death. The literal rendering lets the reader hear that link.

The verb can mean that the kingdom has drawn close but has not yet come, or that it has in effect arrived. Scholars dispute which is meant, and the rendering leaves the question open as the Greek does. 'Kingdom' here leans toward God's active reign more than a territory.
These were not copyists but trained scholars and teachers of the Law of Moses, the recognised experts in interpreting it. The contrast is between their learned teaching and Jesus's direct authority.
The day described is a Sabbath (verse 21), which ended at sunset. Carrying the sick was regarded as work forbidden on the Sabbath, so the townspeople wait until the day is over before bringing them.

The Greek term covers a range of scaly skin conditions, not only the disease now called leprosy (Hansen's disease). Under Leviticus 13–14 such conditions made a person ritually unclean and excluded from the community until a priest certified recovery. This is why the man asks to be made clean, and why he is sent to the priest.

The great majority of manuscripts read 'moved with compassion', and most English translations follow them. A few witnesses read 'angered', which the SBLGNT adopts on the ground that a copyist would more readily soften anger into compassion than the reverse. The question is disputed. If 'angered' is original, the anger is not explained and may be directed at the disease and what it has done to the man.
